claim: Antigen detection in vivo has relied on fluorescent conjugation or indirect read-outs such as antigen presentation.
source: In our studies, we found that these widely used techniques had several technical limitations that have precluded a complete picture of antigen trafficking or retention across lymph node cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background context for the study.

claim: Widely used antigen detection techniques have technical limitations that preclude a complete picture of antigen trafficking or retention across lymph node cell types.
source: In our studies, we found that these widely used techniques had several technical limitations that have precluded a complete picture of antigen trafficking or retention across lymph node cell types.
evidence: The authors state this as a finding from their studies.

claim: A molecular tracking device was developed to follow the distribution, acquisition, and retention of antigen in the lymph node.
source: To address these limitations, we developed a 'molecular tracking device' to follow the distribution, acquisition, and retention of antigen in the lymph node.
evidence: This is the main methodological contribution stated in the abstract.

claim: The molecular tracking device utilizes an antigen conjugated to a nuclease-resistant DNA tag.
source: Utilizing an antigen conjugated to a nuclease-resistant DNA tag, acting as a combined antigen-adjuvant conjugate, and single-cell mRNA sequencing, we quantified antigen abundance in the lymph node.
evidence: The abstract describes the composition of the tracking device.

claim: The antigen-DNA conjugate acts as a combined antigen-adjuvant conjugate.
source: Utilizing an antigen conjugated to a nuclease-resistant DNA tag, acting as a combined antigen-adjuvant conjugate, and single-cell mRNA sequencing, we quantified antigen abundance in the lymph node.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this dual function.

claim: Single-cell mRNA sequencing was used to quantify antigen abundance in the lymph node.
source: Utilizing an antigen conjugated to a nuclease-resistant DNA tag, acting as a combined antigen-adjuvant conjugate, and single-cell mRNA sequencing, we quantified antigen abundance in the lymph node.
evidence: The abstract describes the methodology used.

claim: Variable antigen levels enabled the identification of caveolar endocytosis as a mechanism of antigen acquisition or retention in lymphatic endothelial cells.
source: Variable antigen levels enabled the identification of caveolar endocytosis as a mechanism of antigen acquisition or retention in lymphatic endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Small soluble proteins and virus particles pass through the lymphatics to the lymph node after subcutaneous immunization.
source: Upon subcutaneous immunization, small soluble proteins and virus particles pass through the lymphatics to the lymph node (LN), where LN-resident DCs acquire and present antigen (Manolova et al., 2008; Gerner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LN-resident DCs acquire and present antigen that passes through the lymphatics to the lymph node.
source: Upon subcutaneous immunization, small soluble proteins and virus particles pass through the lymphatics to the lymph node (LN), where LN-resident DCs acquire and present antigen (Manolova et al., 2008; Gerner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Larger antigens and/or pathogens that are too large to pass through the lymphatic capillaries require dermal DCs to migrate to the LN for presentation.
source: For larger antigens and/or pathogens that are too large to pass through the lymphatic capillaries, dermal DCs migrate to the LN for presentation of processed antigens to naive T cells (Manolova et al., 2008; Bonneau et al., 2006; Hampton and Chtanova, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most adaptive immune responses require antigen processing and presentation by conventional DCs in either the draining LN or at the site of infection or vaccination.
source: Most adaptive immune responses require antigen processing and presentation by conventional DCs in either the draining LN or at the site of infection or vaccination (migratory cutaneous or dermal DCs) (Eisenbarth, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Viral antigens persist in the LN beyond the time frame of infectious virus.
source: Previous studies have shown that viral antigens persist in the LN beyond the time frame of infectious virus (Jelley-Gibbs et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2011; Takamura et al., 2010; Woodland and Kohlmeier, 2009; Zammit et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Lymphatic endothelial cells store antigens from viral infection and vaccination.
source: We recently found that lymphatic endothelial cells (LEC) store antigens from viral infection and vaccination (Kedl et al., 2017; Kedl and Tamburini, 2015; Tamburini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Antigens are durably retained in the LN after TLR/αCD40 vaccination or viral infection.
source: Using a vaccine formulation that elicits robust cell-mediated immunity comprising antigen, a Toll-like receptor (TLR) agonist, and an agonistic αCD40 antibody (TLR/αCD40 vaccination) or viral infection (Ahonen et al., 2004; Ahonen et al., 2008; Badovinac et al., 2002; Corbin and Harty, 2004; Kaech and Ahmed, 2001; Kurche et al., 2010; Kurche et al., 2012; Lucas et al., 2018; McWilliams et al., 2010; Sanchez and Kedl, 2012; Sanchez et al., 2007; Tamburini et al., 2012), we discovered that antigens were durably retained in the LN (Kedl et al., 2017; Kedl and Tamburini, 2015; Tamburini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Antigen storage is dependent on the presence of a TLR agonist.
source: Antigen storage was dependent on the presence of a TLR agonist (e.g. polyI:C alone [TLR3/MDA5/RIGI or Pam3cys (TLR1/2)+ αCD40]), but also occurred with antigen conjugated to a TLR agonist (e.g. 3M019 [TLR7]) [Tamburini et al., 2014].
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: Antigen archiving is important to poise memory T cells for future antigenic encounters.
source: We named this process 'antigen archiving' and showed it is important to poise memory T cells for future antigenic encounters (Tamburini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: Follicular DCs harbor antigens in antigen-antibody complexes for extended periods of time for the benefit of B cell memory.
source: Prior to these studies, the only non-hematopoietic cell type thought to retain antigens were follicular DCs, which harbor antigens in antigen-antibody complexes for extended periods of time and for the benefit of B cell memory (Zammit et al., 2006; Heesters et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fibroblasts and non-endothelial stromal cells comprise a large portion of the LN stroma.
source: Fibroblasts and non-endothelial stromal cells (SCs) comprise a large portion of the LN stroma and are capable of presenting peripheral tissue antigens, but their capacity to acquire and present foreign antigens is not yet well understood (Fletcher et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2011; Turley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fibroblasts and non-endothelial stromal cells are capable of presenting peripheral tissue antigens.
source: Fibroblasts and non-endothelial stromal cells (SCs) comprise a large portion of the LN stroma and are capable of presenting peripheral tissue antigens, but their capacity to acquire and present foreign antigens is not yet well understood (Fletcher et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2011; Turley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The capacity of fibroblasts and non-endothelial stromal cells to acquire and present foreign antigens is not yet well understood.
source: Fibroblasts and non-endothelial stromal cells (SCs) comprise a large portion of the LN stroma and are capable of presenting peripheral tissue antigens, but their capacity to acquire and present foreign antigens is not yet well understood (Fletcher et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2011; Turley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Antigen archiving by blood endothelial cells or fibroblasts was not detected in initial studies.
source: We were unable to detect antigen archiving by blood endothelial cells (BECs) or fibroblasts in our initial studies (Kedl et al., 2017; Kedl and Tamburini, 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by citations.

claim: LECs present antigens in the absence of inflammation to induce T cell tolerance.
source: While LECs have been shown to present antigens in the absence of inflammation to induce T cell tolerance (Cohen et al., 2010; Cohen et al., 2014; Nichols et al., 2007; Rouhani et al., 2015; Tewalt et al., 2012; Dubrot et al., 2014; Hirosue et al., 2014; Lund et al., 2012), we showed that presentation of archived antigen occurs only after exchange of the archived antigen from an LEC to a migratory DC; changing the stimulus from tolerizing to immunostimulatory (Kedl et al., 2017; Kedl and Tamburini, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Presentation of archived antigen occurs only after exchange of the archived antigen from an LEC to a migratory DC, changing the stimulus from tolerizing to immunostimulatory.
source: While LECs have been shown to present antigens in the absence of inflammation to induce T cell tolerance (Cohen et al., 2010; Cohen et al., 2014; Nichols et al., 2007; Rouhani et al., 2015; Tewalt et al., 2012; Dubrot et al., 2014; Hirosue et al., 2014; Lund et al., 2012), we showed that presentation of archived antigen occurs only after exchange of the archived antigen from an LEC to a migratory DC; changing the stimulus from tolerizing to immunostimulatory (Kedl et al., 2017; Kedl and Tamburini, 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Soluble antigens are exchanged via direct exchange between LECs and migratory DCs.
source: Soluble antigens are exchanged via two distinct mechanisms: (i) direct exchange between LECs and migratory DCs and (ii) LEC death.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism of antigen exchange.

claim: Soluble antigens are exchanged via LEC death.
source: Soluble antigens are exchanged via two distinct mechanisms: (i) direct exchange between LECs and migratory DCs and (ii) LEC death.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism of antigen exchange.

claim: Antigen transfer from LECs to both migratory cDC1s and cDC2s is required for archived antigen presentation to antigen-specific memory T cells.
source: Antigen transfer from LECs to both migratory conventional (c)DC1s and cDC2s is required for archived antigen presentation to antigen-specific memory T cells (Kedl et al., 2017; Kedl and Tamburini, 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by citations.

claim: After viral infection, archived antigen is transferred to Batf3-dependent migratory DCs as a result of LEC death during LN contraction.
source: After viral infection, archived antigen is transferred to Batf3-dependent migratory DCs as a result of LEC death during LN contraction (Kedl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: Limitations of current approaches have precluded sensitive and quantitative measures of antigen levels across cell types.
source: Limitations of current approaches have precluded sensitive and quantitative measures of antigen levels across cell types, providing only a glimpse of the cell types and molecular mechanisms that control antigen acquisition, processing, and retention in the LN.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: Studies of antigen in the LN and peripheral tissues have mainly relied on antigen-fluorophore conjugates or indirect measurement of antigen uptake and presentation.
source: Studies of antigen in the LN and peripheral tissues have mainly relied on antigen-fluorophore conjugates or indirect measurement of antigen uptake and presentation (Gerner et al., 2017; Jelley-Gibbs et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2010; Zammit et al., 2006; Kedl et al., 2017; Tamburini et al., 2014; Jelley-Gibbs et al., 2007), which defined antigen acquisition by specific DC subsets and trafficking of antigens using live imaging (Gerner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Antigen-fluorophore conjugates suffer from low microscopic detection sensitivity, yielding weak signals that diminish over time.
source: However, antigen archiving has been difficult to study because antigen-fluorophore conjugates suffer from low microscopic detection sensitivity, yielding weak signals that diminish over time.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of fluorophore conjugates.

claim: Detection of antigen in the LN and other tissues has relied on flow cytometric analysis using cell surface markers, restricting analysis to specific cell types.
source: Moreover, detection of antigen in the LN and other tissues has relied on flow cytometric analysis using cell surface markers, restricting analysis to specific cell types.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: The phosphorothioate DNA contained a tracking device for detection using single-cell mRNA sequencing and initiated a robust immune response when conjugated to the protein antigen.
source: The phosphorothioate DNA contained a tracking device for detection using single-cell mRNA sequencing and initiated a robust immune response when conjugated to the protein antigen.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the developed system.

claim: The ~60 nt DNA tag contains a unique sequence barcode and PCR primer binding sites, similar to CITE-seq tags.
source: The ~60 nt DNA tag contains a unique sequence barcode and PCR primer binding sites, similar to CITE-seq tags (Stoeckius et al., 2017; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the composition of the DNA tag, with a citation to CITE-seq.

claim: Quality control of ova-DNA conjugates indicated a 1:1 stoichiometry of protein to DNA.
source: Quality control of these conjugates indicated a 1:1 stoichiometry of protein to DNA (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Significantly higher levels of ova-psDNA were found in BMDCs relative to ova-pDNA at day 1 (approximately fourfold; p=0.002).
source: We found significantly higher levels of ova-psDNA in cells relative to ova-pDNA (approximately fourfold at day 1; p=0.002 and approximately sevenfold at day 3; p=0.004), indicating that psDNA is more stable than pDNA (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Significantly higher levels of ova-psDNA were found in BMDCs relative to ova-pDNA at day 3 (approximately sevenfold; p=0.004).
source: We found significantly higher levels of ova-psDNA in cells relative to ova-pDNA (approximately fourfold at day 1; p=0.002 and approximately sevenfold at day 3; p=0.004), indicating that psDNA is more stable than pDNA (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: psDNA is more stable than pDNA in BMDCs.
source: We found significantly higher levels of ova-psDNA in cells relative to ova-pDNA (approximately fourfold at day 1; p=0.002 and approximately sevenfold at day 3; p=0.004), indicating that psDNA is more stable than pDNA (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is inferred from the higher levels of ova-psDNA detected over time.

claim: Ova conjugation is required for phagocytosis by BMDCs as limited amounts of unconjugated pDNA or psDNA were detected (values <1 at days 1–7).
source: In addition, ova conjugation was required for phagocytosis by BMDCs as we detected limited amounts of unconjugated pDNA or psDNA (values <1 at days 1–7) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Both ova and DNA were detected within the same BMDCs by flow cytometry.
source: To determine if the BMDCs had both the ova and DNA within each cell, we used flow cytometry and immunofluorescence using an antibody to detect ova and streptavidin to detect the biotinylated DNA tag. We detected both ova and DNA within the same cells by flow cytometry (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) and co-localization by immunofluorescence (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Ova and DNA co-localize within BMDCs by immunofluorescence.
source: To determine if the BMDCs had both the ova and DNA within each cell, we used flow cytometry and immunofluorescence using an antibody to detect ova and streptavidin to detect the biotinylated DNA tag. We detected both ova and DNA within the same cells by flow cytometry (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) and co-localization by immunofluorescence (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Ova-psDNA conjugates were stable over 7 days of culture in mouse LECs.
source: We also measured conjugate stability in mouse LECs, a cell type that retains foreign proteins for long periods (Tamburini et al., 2014), and found that ova-psDNA conjugates were stable over 7 days of culture, whereas ova-pDNA was rapidly degraded (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Ova-pDNA was rapidly degraded in mouse LECs.
source: We also measured conjugate stability in mouse LECs, a cell type that retains foreign proteins for long periods (Tamburini et al., 2014), and found that ova-psDNA conjugates were stable over 7 days of culture, whereas ova-pDNA was rapidly degraded (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The ova protein and the barcode were detected within the same endothelial cell and co-localized to the same location.
source: In the endothelial cells, we detected both the ova protein and the barcode within the same cell and co-localized to same location (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, c.

claim: The ova-psDNA retention within the LECs was similar to a vaccine strategy using an ova protein-fluorophore conjugate with polyI:C and anti-CD40.
source: Furthermore, the ova-psDNA retention within the LECs was similar to a vaccine strategy using an ova protein-fluorophore conjugate with polyI:C and anti-CD40, which we previously demonstrated induces antigen archiving (Tamburini et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–f and a citation.

claim: Nearly all bone marrow-derived macrophages phagocytosed the ova-psDNA at day 1.
source: Using a more phagocytic cell, bone marrow-derived macrophages, we observed nearly all macrophages phagocytosed the ova-psDNA at day 1 and found the ova and psDNA within the same cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: In macrophages given ova-psDNA 7 days prior, only ova protein was detected.
source: In macrophages given ova-psDNA 7 days prior, we detected only ova protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g), potentially resulting from high levels of endonucleases found within the lysosome of macrophages (Krieser et al., 2002; Nagata, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g and citations.

claim: High levels of endonucleases are found within the lysosome of macrophages.
source: In macrophages given ova-psDNA 7 days prior, we detected only ova protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g), potentially resulting from high levels of endonucleases found within the lysosome of macrophages (Krieser et al., 2002; Nagata, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BMDCs given ova-psDNA induced significantly more proliferation of OT1 T cells than unconjugated ova.
source: BMDCs given ova-psDNA induced significantly more proliferation of OT1 T cells than unconjugated ova (Figure 1g, h), suggesting enhanced activation of BMDCs upon encounter with ova-psDNA conjugates.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1g, h.

claim: Ova-psDNA conjugates suggest enhanced activation of BMDCs upon encounter.
source: BMDCs given ova-psDNA induced significantly more proliferation of OT1 T cells than unconjugated ova (Figure 1g, h), suggesting enhanced activation of BMDCs upon encounter with ova-psDNA conjugates.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased T cell proliferation.

claim: pDNA and psDNA were detected in BMDC culture media at 1 day after addition but not at later time points.
source: Furthermore, we detected pDNA and psDNA in BMDC culture media at 1 day after addition but not at later time points, confirming that ova-psDNA conjugates are processed and not released by BMDCs after phagocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b.

claim: Ova-psDNA conjugates are processed and not released by BMDCs after phagocytosis.
source: Furthermore, we detected pDNA and psDNA in BMDC culture media at 1 day after addition but not at later time points, confirming that ova-psDNA conjugates are processed and not released by BMDCs after phagocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of DNA in media at later time points.

claim: Ova-psDNA conjugates led to increased OT1 proliferation relative to ova plus psDNA (unconjugated).
source: Finally, ova-psDNA conjugates led to increased OT1 proliferation relative to ova plus psDNA (unconjugated), showing that ova-psDNA conjugates are immunostimulatory (Figure 1g, h) and consistent with studies showing conjugation of antigens to RNA or DNA induce TLR7 (RNA) or TLR9 (DNA) signals that lead to prolonged antigen presentation (Xu and Moyle, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1g, h.

claim: Ova-psDNA conjugates are immunostimulatory.
source: Finally, ova-psDNA conjugates led to increased OT1 proliferation relative to ova plus psDNA (unconjugated), showing that ova-psDNA conjugates are immunostimulatory (Figure 1g, h) and consistent with studies showing conjugation of antigens to RNA or DNA induce TLR7 (RNA) or TLR9 (DNA) signals that lead to prolonged antigen presentation (Xu and Moyle, 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased T cell proliferation and supported by a citation.

claim: Conjugation of antigens to RNA or DNA induce TLR7 (RNA) or TLR9 (DNA) signals that lead to prolonged antigen presentation.
source: Finally, ova-psDNA conjugates led to increased OT1 proliferation relative to ova plus psDNA (unconjugated), showing that ova-psDNA conjugates are immunostimulatory (Figure 1g, h) and consistent with studies showing conjugation of antigens to RNA or DNA induce TLR7 (RNA) or TLR9 (DNA) signals that lead to prolonged antigen presentation (Xu and Moyle, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Addition of polyI:C and anti-CD40 to BMDCs with ova elicited robust OT1 proliferation.
source: Addition of polyI:C and anti-CD40 to BMDCs with ova also elicited robust OT1 proliferation, demonstrating that TLR activation on the BMDCs is required for efficient cross-presentation to T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c.

claim: TLR activation on BMDCs is required for efficient cross-presentation to T cells.
source: Addition of polyI:C and anti-CD40 to BMDCs with ova also elicited robust OT1 proliferation, demonstrating that TLR activation on the BMDCs is required for efficient cross-presentation to T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is inferred from the robust OT1 proliferation upon TLR activation.

claim: T cell responses to ova-psDNA were greater than ova with polyI:C.
source: We compared antigen-specific T cell responses in mice vaccinated with a mixture of ova-psDNA and polyI:C/αCD40 to its individual components (ova, psDNA, polyI:C, and polyI:C/αCD40; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b) and—consistent with the differences in OT1 proliferation we saw in vitro—found that T cell responses to ova-psDNA were greater than either ova with polyI:C, ova with polyI:C/αCD40, or a mixture of unconjugated ova and psDNA (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: T cell responses to ova-psDNA were greater than ova with polyI:C/αCD40.
source: We compared antigen-specific T cell responses in mice vaccinated with a mixture of ova-psDNA and polyI:C/αCD40 to its individual components (ova, psDNA, polyI:C, and polyI:C/αCD40; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b) and—consistent with the differences in OT1 proliferation we saw in vitro—found that T cell responses to ova-psDNA were greater than either ova with polyI:C, ova with polyI:C/αCD40, or a mixture of unconjugated ova and psDNA (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: T cell responses to ova-psDNA were greater than a mixture of unconjugated ova and psDNA.
source: We compared antigen-specific T cell responses in mice vaccinated with a mixture of ova-psDNA and polyI:C/αCD40 to its individual components (ova, psDNA, polyI:C, and polyI:C/αCD40; Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b) and—consistent with the differences in OT1 proliferation we saw in vitro—found that T cell responses to ova-psDNA were greater than either ova with polyI:C, ova with polyI:C/αCD40, or a mixture of unconjugated ova and psDNA (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Ova-psDNA conjugate combined with polyI:C/αCD40 did not significantly enhance the T cell response beyond ova-psDNA alone.
source: Interestingly, ova-psDNA conjugate combined with polyI:C/αCD40 did not significantly enhance the T cell response beyond ova-psDNA alone (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: T cells stimulated by ova-psDNA produced significantly more IFNγ than any other vaccination strategy even in the absence of ex vivo SIINFEKL peptide stimulation.
source: T cells stimulated by ova-psDNA produced significantly more IFNγ than any other vaccination strategy even in the absence of ex vivo SIINFEKL peptide stimulation, indicating prolonged and active presentation of ova-psDNA (Figure 2c, d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c, d.

claim: Prolonged and active presentation of ova-psDNA occurs in vivo.
source: T cells stimulated by ova-psDNA produced significantly more IFNγ than any other vaccination strategy even in the absence of ex vivo SIINFEKL peptide stimulation, indicating prolonged and active presentation of ova-psDNA (Figure 2c, d).
evidence: This is inferred from the high IFNγ production without ex vivo stimulation.

claim: Ova-psDNA conjugates elicit antigen-specific T cell responses independent of polyI:C/αCD40.
source: Together, these data show that ova-psDNA conjugates elicit antigen-specific T cell responses independent of polyI:C/αCD40.
evidence: This is inferred from the T cell response data.

claim: The findings are consistent with TLR9-dependent immune responses elicited by psDNA.
source: These findings are consistent with TLR9-dependent immune responses elicited by psDNA (Baek et al., 2001; Coffman et al., 2010; Vollmer et al., 2004), similar to DC presentation of conjugates of ova demonstrated with other TLR agonists (van Montfoort et al., 2009) and other subcutaneously administered ova-TLR conjugate vaccine platforms (Xu and Moyle, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Subcutaneously administered ova-psDNA alone elicited a T cell response.
source: To evaluate antigen-psDNA performance during an active infection, we determined T cell responses after vaccination by comparing individual components with mixtures of ova, VV, ova-pDNA, or ova-psDNA. Subcutaneously administered ova-psDNA alone again elicited a T cell response (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), and addition of VV to ova-psDNA conjugate moderately increased T cell responses compared to ova-psDNA alone, similar to what we observed with ova-psDNA/polyI:C/αCD40 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Addition of VV to ova-psDNA conjugate moderately increased T cell responses compared to ova-psDNA alone.
source: To evaluate antigen-psDNA performance during an active infection, we determined T cell responses after vaccination by comparing individual components with mixtures of ova, VV, ova-pDNA, or ova-psDNA. Subcutaneously administered ova-psDNA alone again elicited a T cell response (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), and addition of VV to ova-psDNA conjugate moderately increased T cell responses compared to ova-psDNA alone, similar to what we observed with ova-psDNA/polyI:C/αCD40 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: CD45- stromal cells had high amounts of ova-psDNA 7 days after vaccination.
source: We found that CD45- SCs had high amounts of ova-psDNA, but not ova-pDNA, corresponding to increased inflammation (Tamburini et al., 2014), whereas CD45+ leukocytes had very low levels of ova-psDNA or ova-pDNA 7 days after vaccination (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: CD45- stromal cells did not have high amounts of ova-pDNA 7 days after vaccination.
source: We found that CD45- SCs had high amounts of ova-psDNA, but not ova-pDNA, corresponding to increased inflammation (Tamburini et al., 2014), whereas CD45+ leukocytes had very low levels of ova-psDNA or ova-pDNA 7 days after vaccination (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: CD45+ leukocytes had very low levels of ova-psDNA or ova-pDNA 7 days after vaccination.
source: We found that CD45- SCs had high amounts of ova-psDNA, but not ova-pDNA, corresponding to increased inflammation (Tamburini et al., 2014), whereas CD45+ leukocytes had very low levels of ova-psDNA or ova-pDNA 7 days after vaccination (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Ova-psDNA, but not ova-pDNA, is a faithful tracking device for antigen archiving in vivo.
source: These data recapitulate our previous demonstration of durable antigen retention by CD45- SCs (Kedl et al., 2017; Tamburini et al., 2014), confirming that ova-psDNA, but not ova-pDNA, is a faithful tracking device for antigen archiving in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing ova-psDNA retention in CD45- SCs.

claim: A total of 800 cells were recovered in the CD45- fraction at the 2-day time point.
source: We recovered a total of 800 cells in the CD45- fraction and 8187 cells in the CD45+ fraction at the 2-day time point.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of cells recovered.

claim: A total of 8187 cells were recovered in the CD45+ fraction at the 2-day time point.
source: We recovered a total of 800 cells in the CD45- fraction and 8187 cells in the CD45+ fraction at the 2-day time point.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of cells recovered.

claim: More CD45- cells (6372 CD45-; 4840 CD45+) were recovered at the 14-day time point likely due to expansion and proliferation of the LN stroma.
source: We recovered more CD45- cells (6372 CD45-; 4840 CD45+) at the 14-day time point likely due to expansion and proliferation of the LN stroma (Tamburini et al., 2014; Lucas et al., 2018; Lucas and Tamburini, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VV mRNAs were not recovered in cells at either time point.
source: We did not recover VV mRNAs in cells at either time point, possibly due to viral clearance or a failure to recover infected, apoptotic cells in the live/dead selection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of what was not detected.

claim: Conventional DCs, including cDC1 and cDC2, were detected at day 2.
source: We detected conventional DCs, including cDC1 and cDC2 (Figure 3a–c), which develop from a common DC precursor upon expression of FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 ligand (Flt3L) (Guilliams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a–c and a citation.

claim: cDC1 and cDC2 develop from a common DC precursor upon expression of Flt3L.
